claims.text: Combining DSC, in situ high-temperature XRD, dilatometry, CALPHAD, and atomistic simulations will determine melting temperature with less than 5% error across a wide range of high-entropy alloys.
The integrated approach will determine fusion enthalpy with less than 5% error across a wide range of high-entropy alloys.
The integrated approach will determine fusion entropy with less than 5% error across a wide range of high-entropy alloys.
The integrated approach will determine volume change at melting with less than 5% error across a wide range of high-entropy alloys.
The integrated approach will determine liquid-phase thermodynamic properties with less than 5% error across a wide range of high-entropy alloys.
The combined experimental and computational approach will determine the listed properties efficiently.
Computational modeling can be used to cross-validate and correct thermal and structural measurements from DSC, in situ XRD, and dilatometry.
Convergence between experimentally determined phase boundaries and computationally predicted melting points links structural transitions to thermodynamic parameters.
Cross-validation of thermal events using multiple experimental methods and simulations minimizes uncertainty caused by sluggish kinetics.
Cross-validation of thermal events using multiple experimental methods and simulations minimizes uncertainty caused by metastable phenomena.
Minimizing kinetic and metastability-related uncertainties produces robust, low-error thermodynamic-property determinations.
Measurements from the integrated approach will agree with simulation predictions within approximately 5%.
Agreement between measurements and simulations will reveal consistent trends in melting and liquid-phase properties across the high-entropy-alloy family.
Standalone single-technique methods such as DSC typically have errors exceeding 10%.
The higher errors of standalone methods arise from calibration limitations and difficulty capturing transient phase transitions.
The approach is applicable to high-quality high-entropy alloys studied under well-calibrated, controlled laboratory conditions.
Extreme kinetic hindrances or suboptimal calibration reduce the applicability of the approach.
Highly heterogeneous or rapidly evolving alloy systems can pose additional challenges and affect attainable error margins.
In situ high-temperature XRD can supply phase-transition and liquidus-line determinations for the proposed validation.
The approach is falsified if more than 75% of tested compositions show experimental-to-computational deviations greater than 10%.

contradictions.description: The main performance claim is less than or approximately 5% error, but the falsification rule only rejects the approach when more than 75% of compositions deviate by over 10%. Thus, results that clearly fail the stated 5% target could nevertheless pass the proposed validation rule.
